outcome: Since 26 January 2024, two preprints posted in September 2026 each give an embedded, non-convex, genus-3 polyhedral surface with eight nonagonal faces in which every pair of faces shares at least one edge: Mizhaev (arXiv:2609.17700, submitted 15 Sep 2026) and Röst and Vígh (arXiv:2609.32998, submitted 26 Sep 2026). So the eight-face case is instanced under that reading. In both examples eight of the 28 face pairs share two edges, so whether they satisfy the question depends on the face-adjacency convention, and neither has been peer reviewed or independently checked.
problem_asks: Parts: (1) there exists a polyhedron; (2) it is non-convex; (3) it has no self-intersections; (4) it has more than seven faces; (5) every pair of its faces shares an edge with each other. Read literally, one example with eight or more faces answers the question affirmatively, and a negative answer would have to exclude every face count above seven. Not fixed by the wording: the genus (nothing restricts it, so tori and higher-genus surfaces are not excluded by the text); whether 'polyhedron' requires faces to be simple, planar or convex; whether 'share an edge' means exactly one common edge or at least one; and whether two faces may meet in two edges. Context from the Wikipedia Szilassi polyhedron article (read through a summarising fetch): the tetrahedron (convex, four faces) and the Szilassi polyhedron (genus 1, seven hexagonal faces) are the only known polyhedra in which every pair of faces is adjacent.

events.what_happened: Ruslan Mizhaev (independent researcher), 'Integer realization of an equivelar octahedron of genus 3', arXiv:2609.17700, math.CO and math.GT, v1 submitted 15 Sep 2026 (5 pages, 2 figures, 'includes exact integer coordinate tables'; the arXiv abstract page lists only v1). Abstract (quoted through a summarising fetch): 'We present an integer-coordinate realization of a genus-3 polyhedral surface with eight planar simple nonagonal faces.' It has 24 vertices, 36 edges, three faces at each vertex (type {9,3}), C4 symmetry. The author states that exact integer verification confirms planar faces, a closed orientable surface, and 'no unintended intersections'. Press coverage: Gizmodo (29 Sep 2026), New Scientist (25 Sep, reported second-hand), PopSci, t3n (11 Oct), Eigen Radar (26 Sep), ex.rs (Arthur Breitman, 29 Sep), NerdNews (5 Oct). Press gives 26 edges in several places; the paper and MathWorld give 36, which the Euler characteristic 24 − 36 + 8 = −4 (genus 3) requires.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the arXiv abstract page as of 12 Oct 2026. The PDF could not be read through the fetch tool, so the text used here is from the HTML version.
events.delivers: An embedded genus-3 polyhedral surface with exactly eight faces: eight planar simple nonagonal faces, 24 vertices, 36 edges, every face pair meeting. Per the paper's own definition (as quoted by the summariser: a polyhedral surface is a finite collection of planar polygonal faces whose pairwise intersections are empty, a common vertex or a common edge), 20 face pairs share one edge and 8 pairs share two (disjoint) edges, so the intersections are edges rather than single edges. Non-convexity follows from genus 3, since a convex polyhedron has genus 0. Restrictions: eight faces only, genus 3, C4 symmetry, integer coordinates. MathWorld notes that the example uses the cellular-embedding convention, not the stricter polyhedral-complex convention in which two faces meet in at most one edge.
events.remains: Under the strict polyhedral-complex convention (two faces meet in at most one edge) this example does not qualify, so the eight-face case is not settled on that reading. Faces other than eight are untouched. The 12-face case with every pair sharing exactly one edge, which Röst and Vígh say remains open, is untouched.

events.directly_checkable: The paper gives integer vertex coordinates, face walks and plane equations (per the search-result summary and the 'exact integer coordinate tables' comment). The planarity and intersection checks are exact integer computations a reader can redo with computer algebra. I found no third-party redo and no code artefact for the flat polyhedron.
events.doubts: (a) The self-intersection and face-intersection claims rest on the author's own exact integer tests. The paper's Section 5 says 'Pairwise intersection tests between the eight planar polygons show that the intersection of two faces is exactly the edge(s) prescribed by the walks' (summariser's quote). No independent check found. (b) Convention: 8 of 28 face pairs share two disjoint edges. MathWorld states the paper uses the cellular-embedding convention rather than the stricter polyhedral-complex convention. (c) Single author; preprint; not peer reviewed; v1 only. (d) The press figure of 26 edges is contradicted by the paper's own count of 36 and by the Euler arithmetic; I treat 26 as a press error.
events.direction: Cuts toward yes for the eight-face case as literally worded (non-convex, self-intersection-free as claimed, eight faces, every pair sharing an edge), provided 'share an edge' allows a pair to share two edges. It does not bear on any other face count.
events.object: A genus-3 polyhedral surface (Euler characteristic 24 − 36 + 8 = −4): eight planar simple nonagonal faces, 24 vertices each on three faces, 36 edges, and all 28 face pairs meeting (20 pairs in one edge, 8 pairs in two disjoint edges). Given as explicit integer vertex coordinates with plane equations and face walks, with C4 symmetry. The author's claim is that the faces meet only along the edges the walks prescribe. Explicit, not a non-constructive existence proof.

events.what_happened: Gergely Röst and Viktor Vígh (University of Szeged), 'A second eight-faced polyhedron in which every two faces share an edge', arXiv:2609.32998, v1 submitted 26 Sep 2026 (22:45 UTC); also deposited on Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23027039, dated 29 Sep 2026 (same paper). Abstract opens 'We report a novel polyhedral surface of genus 3 embedded in R^3' and describes eight planar, simple, non-convex nonagonal faces, 24 vertices and 36 edges, with every two faces sharing at least one edge. They report 20 pairs sharing one edge and 8 pairs sharing two collinear edges, which they call 'doubled pairs'. The example was 'found by a computational geometric search, using significant computational resources' (Section 5), with the algorithm 'implemented in Python', and 'verified through a highly autonomous AI framework'. All properties are verified in exact rational arithmetic; face planes and vertices are rational. They say it has the same face vector and edge-multiplicity counts as Mizhaev's polyhedron but is not combinatorially equivalent to it, and give its symmetry group as D2 of order 4 (a second snippet reports eight orientation-preserving automorphisms, dihedral; I could not reconcile these without the PDF). Their introduction and Section 5 say that flat-faced polyhedra with twelve faces, each pair sharing exactly one edge, remain open, and that it is not known whether further examples exist.
events.revisions: v1 only per the arXiv abstract page. Zenodo deposit dated 29 Sep 2026 is the same paper.
events.delivers: An embedded genus-3 polyhedral surface with eight faces, all 28 face pairs meeting: 20 pairs in one edge, 8 pairs in two collinear edges. Same structural restrictions as Mizhaev's example (genus 3, doubled pairs, eight nonagonal non-convex faces). It is an independent example, not a generalisation. Non-convexity follows from genus 3.
events.remains: Under the strict one-edge-per-pair reading, nothing is delivered for eight faces. The 12-face case with exactly one edge per pair remains open by the authors' own statement. Whether any other face count admits an example is not addressed. The authors do not say whether they regard the Wikipedia question as answered.
events.time_since_posted: 16 days as of 12 Oct 2026. No public engagement found beyond the Zenodo deposit; the press pieces I read (Gizmodo, Eigen Radar, NerdNews, ex.rs) do not cite it.
events.directly_checkable: Yes in principle: rational vertex coordinates and face plane equations. Per the summariser's reading of Section 3, each face pair's intersection is computed on the line where their planes meet. I did not check the coordinates, and no third party has redone the check that I could find.
events.doubts: (a) The only support is the authors' own exact computations and 'verified through a highly autonomous AI framework' (the framework is not named). The authors state they 'reviewed and validated all of its outputs'. No independent check found. (b) The same convention issue: 8 pairs share two collinear edges, so a strict one-edge-per-pair reading excludes it. (c) The symmetry description is inconsistent between sources (D2 of order 4 versus eight orientation-preserving automorphisms, dihedral); I could not resolve this without the PDF. (d) Preprint, not peer reviewed.
events.direction: Cuts toward yes for the eight-face case under the at-least-one-edge reading, the same direction as the Mizhaev example. The authors frame it as a second example of the same phenomenon, not as settling the question.
events.object: A genus-3 embedded polyhedral surface (Euler characteristic −4): eight planar, simple, non-convex nonagonal faces, 24 vertices, 36 edges, every two faces sharing at least one edge (20 pairs in one edge, 8 pairs in two collinear edges). Rational vertex coordinates and face planes; found by computer search and checked in exact rational arithmetic. Explicit rather than a non-constructive existence proof. Not combinatorially equivalent to Mizhaev's polyhedron.

events.what_happened: Lars Schewe, 'Nonrealizable minimal vertex triangulations of surfaces: showing nonrealizability using oriented matroids and satisfiability solvers', arXiv:0801.2582 (first submitted 16 Jan 2008; one version), published in Discrete & Computational Geometry 43 (2010) 289–302 (journal reference as given in the Röst–Vígh reference list; not checked on the journal page). Abstract (read on arXiv): no minimal vertex triangulation of a closed, connected, orientable genus-6 surface admits a polyhedral embedding in R^3; examples of minimal vertex triangulations of genus 5 admit no polyhedral embedding; a new infinite family of non-realizable triangulations. The method is computational (satisfiability solvers and oriented matroids). Röst and Vígh read the genus-6 result as ruling out realisation of the 59 neighbourly 12-vertex triangulations as polyhedra.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only; journal version DCG 43 (2010) 289–302.
events.delivers: Non-realizability as polyhedral embeddings in R^3 of minimal vertex triangulations of genus 6 (on the Röst–Vígh reading, including the 12-vertex neighbourly family) and of some genus-5 triangulations. This is the vertex-triangulation side. It is a different question from face-neighbourly polyhedra.
events.remains: Everything the question asks. Röst and Vígh state that the result does not transfer to the face version, because the dual of an embedded polyhedron need not be embedded. So it excludes no face-neighbourly polyhedron with twelve faces.

Press frames the eight-face shape as a new discovery by Mizhaev in September 2026. summary: The problem's 2026 status turns on two September 2026 preprints. Ruslan Mizhaev (arXiv:2609.17700, v1 15 Sep 2026, single author, not peer reviewed) gives integer coordinates for a genus-3 embedded polyhedral surface with eight planar nonagonal faces, 24 vertices and 36 edges, in which every pair of the eight faces meets: 20 pairs share one edge and 8 pairs share two disjoint edges. Gergely Röst and Viktor Vígh (Szeged; arXiv:2609.32998, v1 26 Sep 2026, not peer reviewed; also on Zenodo) report a second, non-equivalent example with the same counts, which they describe as embedded in R^3, found by computer search and verified in exact rational arithmetic. Both examples are non-convex (genus 3 forces this) and both satisfy 'more than seven faces, every pair sharing an edge' under the reading that a pair may share two edges. Under a strict reading, where two faces meet in at most one edge, neither qualifies and the eight-face case stays open. The Euler-type counting quoted from Wikipedia (h = (f−4)(f−3)/12 for the exactly-one-edge case; my arithmetic gives 1 for f = 7, 6 for f = 12 and 5/3 for f = 8) is consistent with doubled pairs being what makes f = 8 possible at all, but I have not verified that formula against the Wikipedia text. The Wikipedia Szilassi article, read through a summarising fetch that reported a last-edit date of 22 Sep 2026, still poses the question as open and does not mention either 2026 example. Röst and Vígh say the twelve-face case with exactly one edge per pair remains open and that it is not known whether further examples exist. AI involvement: the Mizhaev paper's acknowledgement credits OpenAI's ChatGPT with text translation, formatting and 'assistance with certain calculations' (the paper does not say which calculations, and press reports that it wrote Python scripts, which is press and not recorded as the authors' account). The Röst–Vígh acknowledgement credits 'significant use of artificial intelligence (Claude) in most phases of this work' and says the authors validated all outputs; their search was 'implemented in Python' and 'verified through a highly autonomous AI framework' (unnamed). Their 'most phases' statement is the stronger claim and is recorded as Claude. Earlier events: a 2008 non-realizability result on vertex triangulations (Schewe, DCG 2010), a 2016 non-existence result for immersed vertex triangulations of a non-orientable surface (Leopold, abstract read only), a 2025 numerical study that reports one unsuccessful search for a 12-vertex genus-6 dual (Bokowski and Kevin H., Symmetry 2025, full text unreadable), and the 2002 paper on the seven-face Szilassi torus. None of these bears on a >7-face polyhedron with every pair adjacent. The 2020 OSF preprint by Mizhaev is the largest unresolved item: if it already contains an embedded realisation, the first public written argument predates the window and the 2026 papers are second events. Press coverage (Gizmodo, New Scientist as reported second-hand, PopSci, t3n, Eigen Radar, NerdNews, ex.rs) repeats the 26-edge figure in places and carries no mathematical verification. I found no Quanta, Terence Tao, MathOverflow, Reddit or Hacker News engagement with either example. Qualifications for Röst, Vígh and Schewe come from search snippets; Schewe's Edinburgh affiliation, as reported by the press, could not be confirmed.
competing_reading: The strictest reading of 'polyhedron' treats it as a polyhedral complex in which two faces meet in at most one edge (MathWorld's stricter convention). Under that reading neither 2026 example qualifies, the eight-face case is open, and the count above gives a non-integer for f = 8, so no exactly-one-edge example is possible there on an orientable surface. A second reading concerns dating rather than the convention: if the 2020 OSF text already contains an embedded realisation, the first public written argument moves to 2020, before the window, and both 2026 papers become second events. On the AI question, the Mizhaev acknowledgement ('assistance with certain calculations') may describe peripheral help, which would make the AI contribution incidental; the Röst–Vígh 'most phases' statement is the stronger claim, and whether 'the AI framework' produced load-bearing mathematics or only checked the authors' computations cannot be settled from the paper as I read it.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The intended meaning of 'polyhedron' and of 'share an edge' in the Wikipedia bullet (the original source for the wording, and whether two common edges are allowed). (2) An independent exact check of the coordinates in either preprint, and of the claimed absence of self-intersections in the flat polyhedron (not only the morph). (3) The 2020 OSF text, which decides the first public written argument date. (4) Peer review or journal acceptance of either 2026 paper, and any published commentary by a geometer. (5) The full text of the 2025 Symmetry paper, to see whether any dual it reports is face-neighbourly with more than seven faces. (6) The Röst–Vígh PDF, to settle the D2-versus-dihedral symmetry discrepancy and to identify the 'AI framework' named only as 'highly autonomous'. (7) Any statement by Mizhaev or the Röst–Vígh authors saying how the AI tools were used in the construction step itself, as against verification.

event.what_happened: Ruslan Mizhaev (independent researcher), 'Integer realization of an equivelar octahedron of genus 3', arXiv:2609.17700, math.CO and math.GT, v1 submitted 15 Sep 2026 (5 pages, 2 figures, 'includes exact integer coordinate tables'; the arXiv abstract page lists only v1). Abstract (quoted through a summarising fetch): 'We present an integer-coordinate realization of a genus-3 polyhedral surface with eight planar simple nonagonal faces.' It has 24 vertices, 36 edges, three faces at each vertex (type {9,3}), C4 symmetry. The author states that exact integer verification confirms planar faces, a closed orientable surface, and 'no unintended intersections'. Press coverage: Gizmodo (29 Sep 2026), New Scientist (25 Sep, reported second-hand), PopSci, t3n (11 Oct), Eigen Radar (26 Sep), ex.rs (Arthur Breitman, 29 Sep), NerdNews (5 Oct). Press gives 26 edges in several places; the paper and MathWorld give 36, which the Euler characteristic 24 − 36 + 8 = −4 (genus 3) requires.
event.revisions: v1 only, per the arXiv abstract page as of 12 Oct 2026. The PDF could not be read through the fetch tool, so the text used here is from the HTML version.
event.delivers: An embedded genus-3 polyhedral surface with exactly eight faces: eight planar simple nonagonal faces, 24 vertices, 36 edges, every face pair meeting. Per the paper's own definition (as quoted by the summariser: a polyhedral surface is a finite collection of planar polygonal faces whose pairwise intersections are empty, a common vertex or a common edge), 20 face pairs share one edge and 8 pairs share two (disjoint) edges, so the intersections are edges rather than single edges. Non-convexity follows from genus 3, since a convex polyhedron has genus 0. Restrictions: eight faces only, genus 3, C4 symmetry, integer coordinates. MathWorld notes that the example uses the cellular-embedding convention, not the stricter polyhedral-complex convention in which two faces meet in at most one edge.
event.remains: Under the strict polyhedral-complex convention (two faces meet in at most one edge) this example does not qualify, so the eight-face case is not settled on that reading. Faces other than eight are untouched. The 12-face case with every pair sharing exactly one edge, which Röst and Vígh say remains open, is untouched.

event.time_since_posted: 27 days as of 12 Oct 2026. No peer review. No written verification by a mathematician found; engagement is press coverage, a blog, and the Röst–Vígh citation.
event.directly_checkable: The paper gives integer vertex coordinates, face walks and plane equations (per the search-result summary and the 'exact integer coordinate tables' comment). The planarity and intersection checks are exact integer computations a reader can redo with computer algebra. I found no third-party redo and no code artefact for the flat polyhedron.
event.doubts: (a) The self-intersection and face-intersection claims rest on the author's own exact integer tests. The paper's Section 5 says 'Pairwise intersection tests between the eight planar polygons show that the intersection of two faces is exactly the edge(s) prescribed by the walks' (summariser's quote). No independent check found. (b) Convention: 8 of 28 face pairs share two disjoint edges. MathWorld states the paper uses the cellular-embedding convention rather than the stricter polyhedral-complex convention. (c) Single author; preprint; not peer reviewed; v1 only. (d) The press figure of 26 edges is contradicted by the paper's own count of 36 and by the Euler arithmetic; I treat 26 as a press error.
event.direction: Cuts toward yes for the eight-face case as literally worded (non-convex, self-intersection-free as claimed, eight faces, every pair sharing an edge), provided 'share an edge' allows a pair to share two edges. It does not bear on any other face count.
event.object: A genus-3 polyhedral surface (Euler characteristic 24 − 36 + 8 = −4): eight planar simple nonagonal faces, 24 vertices each on three faces, 36 edges, and all 28 face pairs meeting (20 pairs in one edge, 8 pairs in two disjoint edges). Given as explicit integer vertex coordinates with plane equations and face walks, with C4 symmetry. The author's claim is that the faces meet only along the edges the walks prescribe. Explicit, not a non-constructive existence proof.

events.credibility_reason: The 2020 text was never read. Nothing in the record shows it contains an embedded realisation rather than only the combinatorial map, and the 2026 paper calls itself a coordinate realisation of that earlier work.

8 of the 28 face pairs share two edges. If 'polyhedron' is read strictly, so that two faces meet in at most one edge, the example does not qualify. Embeddedness rests only on the author's own exact checks.
Same convention issue: 8 face pairs share two collinear edges. The only verification is the authors' own exact rational checks plus an unnamed AI framework.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether such a polyhedron exists, so one embedded, non-convex, eight-face example in which every pair of faces shares an edge answers it in full. Both 2026 preprints give such an example, explicitly, with exact integer or rational coordinates, and anyone can check them by computer algebra. That makes each of them whole, checkable and a witness. I marked both doubtful rather than credible for two reasons. First, the record leaves open whether two faces may share two edges, and MathWorld points out the stricter polyhedral-complex convention. Second, neither example has been checked by anyone other than its authors. The literal wording, 'share an edge', is met by pairs sharing at least one edge, so I answered on that reading. AI role: Mizhaev's 'assistance with certain calculations' does not say ChatGPT produced any of the construction, so it is none. Röst and Vígh credit Claude with 'significant use … in most phases' of a work whose result is a construction found by search, and I read that as Claude supplying part of the mathematics, so assisted. This was a close call against none, because the quote never says which part Claude produced. The 2020 OSF preprint is unread, so I gave it no scope and cannot place the construction before the snapshot. The 2008, 2016, 2002 and 2025 events are about vertex triangulations, immersions, the seven-face case, or a failed search, so none of them is the question.
judgement.doubts: (1) Whether doubled-edge face pairs are acceptable under the intended meaning of 'polyhedron' and 'share an edge'. Under the strict reading, neither 2026 example qualifies. (2) The 2020 OSF preprint is unread. If it already gives an embedded realisation, the problem moved before the snapshot. (3) The Röst–Vígh 'assisted' call rests on a broad acknowledgement and does not show what Claude produced. (4) No independent third party has rerun the coordinate checks for either example.
